table.brief: 12 narrow columns of short codes and numbers (monthly values Jan–Dec) plus a name column

understanding.purpose: Compare monthly mean ozone levels across six monitoring stations and reveal each station's seasonal profile.
understanding.reading: Readers find a station in column 1, then scan horizontally across Jan–Dec to see its seasonal rise and fall; they may also compare one month vertically across stations. The month sequence is the main comparative axis.
groups: col 1 Station: row identifier, separate from the measurements
cols 2–13 Jan–Dec: one homogeneous 12-month numeric series; quarters Jan–Mar, Apr–Jun, Jul–Sep, Oct–Dec are conceptual subgroups but all months should share a common width
keep_intact: col 1 station names and the Station header
all one-decimal numeric values and their decimal points
may_wrap: None naturally: station names, month labels and values are single unbreakable tokens; any wrapping is forced splitting. If forced, station names can use extra row height better than numeric cells can.

preferred.name: r0A
preferred.note: Keep every station name, month label and one-decimal value intact on one line, accepting a 724px table with horizontal scrolling.

bad.name: r0B
bad.note: Keep the entire month grid and all values intact, narrowing only Station so the longest station names wrap to a second line; total 703px.
bad.why: The narrower Station column breaks every long station name mid-word ("Riversi/de", "Northg/ate", "Westfi/eld", "Eastwo/od"), making the row identifiers hard to scan; rows become uneven and taller, yet the table still overflows by 344px, so the 21px saving is not worth the legibility loss.

bad.name: r0C
bad.note: Fit the 360px viewport with no scroll by keeping Station readable and squeezing all 12 month columns to slivers, so every month header and value fragments vertically.
bad.why: Squeezing the month columns to 38px wraps 12 of 13 headers and splits nearly every numeric value across lines, with 136 mid-word splits; the table becomes 580px tall and still overflows by 191px, so it fails both fit and readability.

rationale: At 360px the table cannot preserve intact station names, month headers, and one-line numeric values at the same time, so the best design accepts horizontal scrolling rather than corrupting the data. r0A keeps every station name and month label on one line, keeps all values on one line, and gives the twelve month columns near-equal widths because they play the same comparative role. r0B and r0C trade away the most important scanning cues—row identity and numeric integrity—while still overflowing the box. A phone reader must scroll, but with r0A the table remains internally consistent and trustworthy.

general: When a wide table cannot fit, preserve unbroken identifiers and one-line numeric values before minimizing horizontal overflow.
Columns that play the same role—here the twelve months—should stay close in width so readers compare them as a series rather than as unrelated fields.
Row headers are primary navigation; breaking them mid-word damages scanning far more than a wider table or horizontal scroll does.
Uneven row heights caused by wrapping in only some rows disrupt the row rhythm and make comparison slower.
specific: This is a 13-column monthly ozone table on a 360px phone viewport; twelve month columns plus a station label cannot be shown at once without either scrolling or destructive splitting.
The station names are long enough that a 73px content width is the practical minimum; anything narrower breaks them mid-word.
The month columns only need about 31–32px of text width, so 52–53px including padding is enough for intact headers and values.
r0A's 725px table overflows substantially, but the overflow is preferable to the 136 mid-word splits and 580px height of r0C.

tradeoffs: A designer prioritizing minimal horizontal scrolling might be tempted by r0B because it saves about 21px, but it breaks station names and still overflows almost as far, so the tradeoff is poor. One could also argue for a fundamentally different mobile layout—transposing months to rows or using cards—but that is outside the column-width decision.
uncertain: The exact upper bounds for the ranges are judgment calls: wider month columns remain readable but add scrolling, while the lower bounds are firm because below them headers or numbers wrap or split. Reasonable designers could disagree about whether a modest amount of wrapping in secondary labels is acceptable, but not about breaking station identifiers or every numeric value.

critique.good: All 13 columns stay on one line: station names, month headers, and one-decimal values are intact; row heights are a uniform 36px and the horizontal scan across months is clean. It is the minimal no-split layout: Station 94px (73+21) and months 52–53px (31–32+21).
critique.problems: It overflows the 360px box by 365px, so only Station through May (plus a sliver of Jun) is visible; the reader must scroll horizontally to see the rest of the year. The 52/53px month alternation is content-driven and visually almost imperceptible.
critique.cause: The no-split minimum is 724px (94 + six 52px months + six 53px months), which cannot fit 359px. The overflow is the unavoidable cost of keeping every word and number intact. This is the correct trade-off: any fitting design must split month labels and/or values, which is worse for a 12-month comparative scan.

critique.good: Month headers and numeric values remain on one line, and the month columns keep their 52–53px widths.
critique.problems: Every station name is broken mid-word (Riversi/de, Northg/ate, Westfi/eld, Eastwo/od), the row heights jump to 60px, and the row identifiers—the reader's entry point—become hard to parse. It still overflows by 344px.
critique.cause: The Station column is 73px, giving only 52px of text after the 21px padding+border, while the longest name needs 73px. Saving 21px is not worth destroying all six row labels, especially when the table still scrolls almost as far as r0A.

critique.good: Station names stay intact, and the attempt tries to reduce horizontal overflow by narrowing the month columns.
critique.problems: Month headers split into fragments (Ja/n, Fe/b, Ma/r, Ap/r, Ma/y, etc.), numeric values break across lines (24./1, 29./3), there are 136 mid-word splits, row heights balloon to 83px, and the tallest cells reach 3 lines. It still overflows by 191px.
critique.cause: The 38px month columns leave only 17px of text width, far below the 31–32px needed for month abbreviations and the ~29–32px needed for one-decimal values. The squeeze is severe enough to destroy both headers and data, yet it does not even achieve a fit, so the trade-off buys nothing.

review.method: two fresh-context blind reviews; letters shuffled; includes browser auto layout and equal widths as neutral references

r0B.why: The Station column is too narrow: Riverside, Northgate, Westfield and Eastwood break mid-word, so row headers stop reading as units. Months and numbers stay intact and more months are visible, but broken identifiers undermine scanning.

r0A.why: Station names, month headers and numeric cells stay intact. Prioritising the row header and accepting horizontal overflow after about May is a reasonable trade-off for this wide monthly table.

ref_equal.why: All 13 columns are squeezed into 360px by splitting nearly everything: headers become vertical letter stacks and values like 24.1 break across lines, destroying readability and comparison.

ref_auto.why: Like B, it preserves station names and intact month/number cells while accepting horizontal overflow. Row rhythm and header hierarchy are clean, though only part of the year is visible at once.

raw.unsure: B and D look essentially identical in the renders, so exact width differences are hard to distinguish. Also, the choice depends on whether horizontal scrolling is acceptable versus showing more months at the cost of split station names.

r0B.why: Month headers and numeric cells stay intact, and it gains an extra visible month, but the Station column is squeezed into awkward two-line fragments such as Riversi/de, Northg/ate and Westfi/eld, damaging the row identifiers.

ref_auto.why: Station names, month headers and all visible numbers stay intact; month columns are even and the partial next column gives a clear horizontal-scroll cue. Only about five months are visible, but that is the unavoidable 360px compromise.

ref_equal.why: Every column is crushed: station names, month headers and numbers break into vertical letter and digit fragments, so the table cannot be scanned as rows or compared across months.

r0A.why: Like B it preserves station names, month headers and numeric values, but the slightly wider Station side leaves less of the next month visible and uses the narrow viewport a little less efficiently.

raw.unsure: B and D are very close; without exact pixel widths I may be over-reading the small difference in how much of the next month is visible. I am also unsure whether A's extra month justifies its broken station identifiers.

provenance.note: AI visual design judgement; not a human reading study
